paragraphs: This paper studies how a convolutional neural network can work across domains while adding very few parameters for each domain. Its starting observation is that a convolutional filter can be approximated by combining a small collection of building blocks, called dictionary atoms. The authors use this decomposition to separate domain-specific variation from information shared across domains.

Each convolutional layer becomes two convolutional layers with different responsibilities. The first applies spatial filters using atoms specific to the input's domain, aiming to absorb domain variations. The second combines channels using coefficients shared across domains. Training these shared coefficients promotes common semantic information, while the atoms provide a compact place to represent differences.

The authors support this design with theoretical analysis, toy examples, and experiments across datasets and architectures. They report effectiveness for cross-domain performance, joint-domain performance, and domain adaptation. Adding another domain requires only a small dictionary, typically a few hundred extra parameters. The contribution is therefore a concrete way to accommodate domain differences without duplicating an entire network.
neurips-2020-a-dictionary-approach-to-do.tldr: Splitting convolutional filters into domain-specific atoms and shared coefficients supports learning across domains with very few additional parameters.

paragraphs: Optimization becomes difficult when an objective has sharp changes or a highly irregular landscape. This paper introduces Bend, Mix and Release, or BMR, a smoothing method that connects randomized smoothing with the Moreau envelope. Its purpose is to balance the computational simplicity of the former with the approximation quality of the latter.

The authors show that BMR can improve approximation error over randomized smoothing by a multiplicative factor of up to the square root of the search-space dimension, while requiring less computation than the Moreau envelope. For nonconvex objectives, it also widens local minima. This makes narrow regions of the landscape more accessible to optimization methods and supports local exploration.

The paper applies BMR to first-order optimization of nonsmooth convex and nonconvex objectives, and describes it as suitable for distributed computation. Its analysis connects the exploration used by evolution strategies with the regularity of first-order optimization problems. Synthetic experiments illustrate the method's impact, complementing the theoretical account of its computational and approximation tradeoffs.
neurips-2020-a-simple-and-efficient-smoo.tldr: BMR smooths difficult optimization landscapes while balancing computational cost, approximation accuracy, and local exploration.

paragraphs: Autoregressive models describe a joint distribution through a sequence of conditional distributions. Each conditional normally needs to be normalized, which constrains how it can be represented. This paper proposes representing the derivatives of the logarithms of those conditionals instead. These derivatives, called scores, do not themselves require normalization, giving the model greater flexibility.

The resulting autoregressive conditional score model is trained using a new distribution-comparison objective called Composite Score Matching. For this model family, the objective can be evaluated and optimized efficiently without expensive sampling or adversarial training. The approach therefore changes both what the network represents and how the mismatch between model and data is measured.

The authors report greater scalability to high-dimensional data and more stable optimization than previous score-matching algorithms. Their experiments cover synthetic density estimation, image generation, image denoising, and latent-variable models with implicit encoders. Together, these applications demonstrate that the conditional-score formulation can support several modeling tasks while avoiding the normalization constraints that motivated the work.
neurips-2020-autoregressive-score-matchi.tldr: Autoregressive conditional score models gain flexibility by learning conditional log-density derivatives with an efficient score-matching objective.

paragraphs: Saliency methods highlight which inputs matter to a model's prediction, but time series introduce two connected questions: which moments matter, and which features matter at those moments. This paper develops a synthetic time-series benchmark to assess how well saliency methods answer those questions across recurrent networks, temporal convolutional networks, and Transformers.

The evaluation uses multiple metrics covering precision and recall. Precision asks whether highlighted inputs actually contain meaningful signal; recall asks how much of the meaningful signal was identified. Across the experiments, the authors find that the tested architectures and saliency methods generally do not recover feature importance over time reliably or accurately.

The authors identify the mixing of time importance and feature importance as the main source of this failure. They propose temporal saliency rescaling, a two-stage procedure that first estimates the importance of each time step and then estimates feature importance within it. Reported improvements show that explicitly separating these questions can substantially improve saliency maps in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2020-benchmarking-deep-learning-.tldr: A time-series benchmark reveals unreliable saliency maps and shows that separating time-step importance from feature importance can substantially improve them.

paragraphs: Neural Processes use neural networks to learn stochastic processes from data, allowing uncertainty and variation to be modeled through a learned representation. This differs from a traditional workflow in which a user explicitly chooses a prior. However, the paper identifies a potentially restrictive assumption: uncertainty in the process is represented through a single latent variable.

The proposed Bootstrapping Neural Process uses the bootstrap, a classical data-driven technique for estimating uncertainty. This gives the model another way to learn stochastic variation without assuming a particular form for it. The motivation is to make uncertainty modeling more flexible while retaining the broader Neural Process approach of learning from data.

The authors demonstrate the method on several types of data and report robustness when the model and data are mismatched. That finding matters because the proposed change addresses how uncertainty is represented, rather than only how predictions are produced. The evidence supports bootstrapping as a useful extension of Neural Processes when their original uncertainty assumption may be limiting.
neurips-2020-bootstrapping-neural-proces.tldr: Bootstrapping Neural Processes use bootstrap-based uncertainty estimation to increase flexibility and demonstrate robustness to model-data mismatch.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether image generators can build complex concepts by combining simpler ones. Its central idea is to combine probability distributions represented by energy-based models. Sampling from the resulting distribution then produces images corresponding to the combined concepts, connecting a mathematical operation on distributions to a visible change in generated content.

For example, distributions describing smiling faces and male faces can be combined to generate smiling male faces. The approach also supports conjunctions, disjunctions, and negations: combinations expressing that concepts occur together, that alternatives are allowed, or that a concept should be absent. This makes composition a direct part of the generation mechanism.

The authors evaluate these capabilities using natural faces from CelebA and synthetic three-dimensional scenes. They also demonstrate that the model can continually incorporate new concepts and infer combinations of concept properties underlying an image. These results support the use of energy-based models as a framework for both constructing visual concept combinations and reasoning about combinations already present in images.
neurips-2020-compositional-visual-genera.tldr: Energy-based models compose probability distributions to generate images satisfying combinations, alternatives, and negations of visual concepts.

paragraphs: Patch attacks alter pixels within a region of bounded size. This paper develops a defense that can certify, for a given image and attack size, that no such adversarial patch exists. The spatial restriction is central: a patch attacker has less freedom than an attacker who can modify scattered pixels anywhere in an image.

The method builds on smoothing-based robustness approaches but exploits that restriction to obtain larger certificates. It also removes randomization, producing deterministic certificates instead of high-confidence probabilistic ones. The authors report substantially faster training than the existing patch-certification approach based on interval bound propagation, along with certificates at ImageNet scale.

For a 5-by-5 patch on CIFAR-10, the method reaches around 57.6% certified accuracy with around 83.8% clean accuracy. The comparison method reaches at most 30.3% certified accuracy with around 47.8% clean accuracy. These results show improved ordinary classification and certified protection in the reported comparison; the guarantee remains tied to the specified image and bounded patch size.
neurips-2020-de-randomized-smoothing-for.tldr: A deterministic smoothing defense exploits patch geometry to improve certified robustness and scale certification to ImageNet.

paragraphs: Distributed second-order optimization often combines estimates computed by separate machines from small data sketches or batches. Averaging these estimates can be less effective when each is systematically biased relative to the full-data solution. This paper addresses that bias directly, aiming to improve how quickly distributed optimization converges.

The method combines modified data sketches, called surrogate sketches, with a carefully adjusted regularization strength for local computations. The sketches use determinantal point processes, which allow the bias of an inverse-Hessian estimate to be calculated exactly. That calculation provides a principled basis for correcting local estimates before they are combined.

For an objective with l2 regularization strength lambda and local sketch size m, the derived local strength is lambda times one minus d_lambda divided by m. Here, d_lambda is the effective dimension of the Hessian, or of the data matrix for quadratic problems. The authors show that this adjustment eliminates bias in their formulation and report both theoretical and empirical improvements in convergence rates.
neurips-2020-debiasing-distributed-secon.tldr: Surrogate sketches and reduced local regularization remove estimation bias in the proposed formulation and improve distributed second-order convergence.

paragraphs: This paper tackles combinatorial optimization on graphs without labeled solutions. Such problems require discrete choices that satisfy constraints, making it challenging to turn neural predictions into valid answers. The proposed framework uses a neural network to represent a probability distribution over sets, drawing inspiration from the probabilistic method associated with Erdos.

The key is the training objective. The authors show that, with a suitably chosen loss, optimizing the network produces a distribution containing a low-cost, constraint-satisfying integral solution with controlled probability. An integral solution makes the required discrete decisions. The probabilistic existence argument is then derandomized to decode the desired solution.

The framework is demonstrated on maximum clique and local graph clustering, where it produces valid solutions and achieves competitive results on real datasets and difficult synthetic instances. Its significance is the connection between unsupervised neural training and certified solution quality. The guarantee depends on the stated relationship between the loss, the learned distribution, and the decoding procedure.
neurips-2020-erdos-goes-neural-an-unsupe.tldr: An unsupervised neural framework learns distributions over graph solutions and derandomizes an existence guarantee to obtain valid discrete solutions.

paragraphs: A factor graph represents relationships among variables through factors. This paper introduces factor graph grammars, which use graph-replacement rules to describe whole sets of factor graphs. The representation can express a broader class of models than plate notation, dynamic graphical models, case-factor diagrams, and sum-product networks, according to the authors.

The main computational contribution is that inference can operate on the grammar without listing every graph it generates. When variable domains are finite, the authors extend variable elimination to the grammar setting. This supports exact, tractable inference in many situations, even when the grammar describes infinitely many graphs.

The paper also treats a different case: a finite collection of generated graphs whose variables may have infinite domains. Here, the grammar can be converted into one factor graph, making standard inference techniques applicable. These two results distinguish the size of the graph collection from the size of each variable's domain, and show how different finiteness conditions enable different inference strategies.
neurips-2020-factor-graph-grammars-f5193.tldr: Factor graph grammars represent families of graphical models and enable inference without enumerating every generated graph under the stated conditions.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis identifies leading directions of variation in data. This paper develops a federated version that operates asynchronously, uses limited memory, and provides differential privacy. Local updates are computed incrementally through a streaming procedure, allowing the method to estimate r leading components with memory proportional to d times r, where d is data dimensionality.

Privacy is obtained by perturbing the covariance matrix with a nonsymmetric Gaussian random matrix. The authors give a noise-variance order proportional to the square of d divided by sample count, multiplied by log d, and describe this as an improvement over prior work. The algorithm is also invariant to permutations of incoming data, supporting robustness to delayed or failed nodes.

Numerical simulations show performance close to or better than traditional nonfederated algorithms despite the limited-memory setting. They also indicate attractive scaling as more computing resources are added when communication latency is absent. That condition matters: the reported scalability statement explicitly excludes communication delays.
neurips-2020-federated-principal-compone.tldr: A streaming federated PCA algorithm combines limited memory, asynchronous updates, differential privacy, and robustness to incoming-data order.

paragraphs: Deep ensembles combine neural networks trained from different random initializations, providing strong accuracy and calibration. This paper asks whether ensemble members should also differ in their hyperparameters. Its central proposal is to combine diversity in learned weights with diversity in the settings used to train the models.

For performance without prioritizing a computational budget, the authors introduce hyper-deep ensembles. The procedure performs random hyperparameter search across multiple random initializations. For greater parameter efficiency, they introduce hyper-batch ensembles, which build on the layer structure of batch ensembles and self-tuning networks. This second version has notably lower computational and memory costs than typical ensembles.

Experiments on image classification use MLP, LeNet, ResNet 20, and Wide ResNet 28-10 architectures. The authors report improvements over both deep ensembles and batch ensembles. These findings support hyperparameter variation as a useful additional source of ensemble diversity, while the two proposed versions offer different ways to pursue that benefit depending on the importance of resource efficiency.
neurips-2020-hyperparameter-ensembles-fo.tldr: Combining hyperparameter diversity with weight diversity improves image-classification ensembles, with a parameter-efficient variant reducing resource costs.

paragraphs: Scheduling in hospitals and factories requires allocating people or other agents to tasks while respecting time and resource constraints. Human experts handle changing conditions using strategies developed through experience. This paper aims to learn those strategies from demonstrations while preserving both differences among demonstrators and an understandable account of their decisions.

The proposed apprenticeship scheduling algorithm infers personalized embeddings and extracts decision-making criteria into an interpretable representation. Its formulation does not require fixing the number of demonstrator types in advance. This addresses the heterogeneity of expert behavior: the learning system can represent differing approaches within a shared scheduling framework.

The authors report near-perfect learning-from-demonstration accuracy in synthetic domains and 88.22% accuracy in a planning domain using real-world data, outperforming baselines. A user study also finds the resulting models more interpretable and easier to use than neural networks, with p below 0.05. The results support both accurate imitation of demonstrated decisions and improved usability in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2020-interpretable-and-personali.tldr: A personalized scheduling learner extracts interpretable decision rules from heterogeneous demonstrations and reports strong imitation accuracy and usability.

paragraphs: Capsule networks need to determine how represented parts connect to represented objects. This paper replaces repeated local routing between adjacent capsule layers with a probabilistic treatment of uncertainty in those connections. The goal is to make routing more computationally efficient while allowing it to use a broader view of the input.

The proposed network uses variational inference to estimate part-object connections. Global latent variables bring information beyond adjacent layers into the routing process and directly influence the objective being optimized. These variables are updated discriminatively according to the minimum description length principle, making global context part of the learning formulation.

The authors report a significant speedup without sacrificing performance and evaluate the method on tasks that require awareness of pose. In those evaluations, they observe performance improvements over previous approaches alongside greater computational efficiency. The findings support modeling routing uncertainty explicitly as a way to improve capsule networks, with the stated evidence focused on preserving and enhancing their pose-related capabilities.
neurips-2020-introducing-routing-uncerta.tldr: Probabilistic capsule routing uses global context and variational inference to improve computational efficiency and reported pose-aware performance.

paragraphs: Vision-and-language models learn representations that connect images with text. This paper introduces VILLA, a large-scale adversarial training approach for those representations. Training has two stages: task-agnostic adversarial pretraining, followed by adversarial finetuning for a specific task. This brings the same broad training idea into both general representation learning and downstream adaptation.

VILLA applies adversarial perturbations to the embedding space of each modality. The modifications therefore act on internal representations of images and text. To make the approach practical at scale, the authors adopt a strategy called free adversarial training and combine it with KL-divergence regularization, which encourages greater invariance in the embedding space.

The authors apply VILLA to strong existing vision-and-language models and report new state-of-the-art results across several tasks. These include visual question answering, visual commonsense reasoning, image-text retrieval, referring expression comprehension, visual entailment, and NLVR2. The breadth of the reported improvements supports the usefulness of embedding-space adversarial training across multiple forms of combined visual and textual understanding.
neurips-2020-large-scale-adversarial-tra.tldr: VILLA applies adversarial training to image and text embeddings during pretraining and finetuning, improving results across vision-and-language tasks.

paragraphs: This paper gives a theoretical account of adversarial perturbations in a particular family of ReLU networks. The networks have random weights, and their dimensions decrease from one layer to the next. Within that setting, the authors show that most networks have adversarial perturbations near most inputs. Both qualifications are part of the result.

The distance bound is proportional, in big-O terms, to the input's Euclidean norm divided by the square root of input dimension. Relative to the size of the input, the bound therefore shrinks as dimension grows. This formalizes how a perturbation can be small in Euclidean distance while still being adversarial for the network.

The authors also show that such perturbations can be found using gradient flow or gradient descent with sufficiently small steps. The contribution thus covers both existence and a way to locate the perturbations. Under the stated network assumptions, it offers an explanation for the prevalence of adversarial examples and the effectiveness of gradient-based searches.
neurips-2020-most-relu-networks-suffer-f.tldr: For most random ReLU networks with shrinking layer dimensions, most inputs admit small adversarial perturbations discoverable by gradient-based methods.

paragraphs: Dangerous failures in autonomous systems may be rare enough that ordinary real-world testing becomes prohibitively expensive. This paper studies safety evaluation through simulation, with the specific goal of computing the probability of dangerous events. Finding a failure and estimating how often it occurs are both central to that evaluation.

The authors develop a rare-event simulation method combining exploration, exploitation, and optimization. These ingredients support the search for failure modes together with estimation of their occurrence rates. The method is accompanied by rigorous guarantees covering both statistical efficiency and computational efficiency, addressing the reliability of estimation as well as the resources it requires.

Experiments across several scenarios demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The authors emphasize rapid sensitivity analysis and model comparison as useful applications during system development and testing. In this role, the method helps evaluate how estimated danger probabilities respond to changes and how alternative models compare. Its stated contribution concerns probabilistic safety assessment in simulation, where rare events can otherwise be difficult to study efficiently.
neurips-2020-neural-bridge-sampling-for-.tldr: A rare-event simulation method finds autonomous-system failure modes and estimates their probabilities with statistical and computational efficiency guarantees.

paragraphs: Neural networks can fit arithmetic within the numerical range used for training yet struggle to generalize beyond it. Specialized arithmetic units address this problem, but existing units may require positive inputs or represent only some operations. This paper introduces the Neural Power Unit, designed to accept real-number inputs and learn arbitrary power functions in a single layer.

The unit uses complex arithmetic internally without requiring the surrounding network to be converted to complex numbers. This construction expands the range of functions available to an arithmetic unit. The authors also introduce a simplified version, RealNPU, whose structure provides a highly transparent model.

On artificial arithmetic datasets, the authors report better accuracy and sparsity than competing methods. They further demonstrate that RealNPU can discover the governing equations of a dynamical system from data alone. These findings connect the architectural contribution to two uses: learning arithmetic more effectively and producing compact, understandable mathematical descriptions of observed dynamics in the demonstrated setting.
neurips-2020-neural-power-units-89d5e197.tldr: Neural Power Units use complex arithmetic internally to learn power functions, with a transparent variant demonstrated on dynamical-equation discovery.

paragraphs: Sortition selects citizens at random to serve on decision-making panels. Equal random invitations do not automatically produce equal representation, because people differ in their willingness to participate. When demographic groups accept invitations at different rates, the available volunteer pool can depart from the composition of the wider population.

This paper develops a sampling algorithm that aims to restore close-to-equal representation probabilities for individuals while meeting demographic quotas. These are related but distinct objectives: a panel should have an appropriate demographic composition, and individuals should have similar chances of representation. The algorithm explicitly addresses both within the selection process.

The method needs estimates of how likely each volunteer was to participate when invited. Because those probabilities are not directly observable, the authors also show how to learn them. They demonstrate the approach using data from a real sortition panel combined with publicly available population survey information. The resulting contribution joins participation modeling with panel sampling to counter the bias introduced by voluntary participation.
neurips-2020-neutralizing-self-selection.tldr: A panel-selection algorithm uses learned participation probabilities to approach equal individual representation while satisfying demographic quotas.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates a policy's performance using data collected under other behavior. The DICE family addresses this through stationary distribution correction and can work with behavior-agnostic data. Although these estimators share that broad purpose, their different derivations and objectives have made their relationships less apparent.

This paper shows that the estimators can be understood as regularized Lagrangians of the same linear program. That common formulation makes it possible to expand the family systematically, yielding new alternatives that demonstrate improved performance. The unification therefore serves both as an explanation of existing methods and as a way to design additional ones.

The authors examine the expanded estimator space mathematically and empirically. They find that dual solutions allow greater flexibility in balancing optimization stability against estimation bias and generally yield better estimates in practice. The practical message is that choices within the shared formulation affect how reliably optimization proceeds and how accurate the resulting evaluation is; the reported preference for dual solutions is qualified rather than universal.
neurips-2020-off-policy-evaluation-via-t.tldr: A shared regularized-Lagrangian formulation unifies DICE estimators and reveals useful alternatives for balancing stability and estimation bias.

paragraphs: Modern reinforcement-learning algorithms combine techniques such as entropy regularization, smoothing of Q-values, and neural function approximation. Their widespread use does not by itself explain how they affect convergence. This paper studies their effects through approximate dynamic programming, focusing on how errors propagate through successive value updates.

The analysis identifies a tradeoff for value smoothing: it increases algorithmic stability but slows convergence. Entropy regularization has a different effect, reducing overestimation errors while changing the original optimization problem. These findings distinguish two mechanisms that may appear together in an algorithm but influence learning in different ways.

The authors also analyze a combination of the techniques that describes Soft Actor-Critic. This connects the theoretical framework to a widely used algorithm and helps interpret the role of its components. The contribution is an account of what those components trade away as well as what they improve: stability comes with slower progress, while reduced overestimation comes with a modified objective.
neurips-2020-on-the-convergence-of-smoot.tldr: An error-propagation analysis shows how value smoothing and entropy regularization trade convergence speed and the original objective for stability and reduced overestimation.

paragraphs: Dense attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length, which can make it expensive for large inputs. SMYRF approximates attention using balanced clustering, reducing complexity from O(N squared) to O(N log N). It combines locality-sensitive hashing with asymmetric transformations and an adaptive procedure that produces balanced clusters.

A central practical benefit is compatibility with pretrained models: SMYRF can replace dense attention without retraining. The authors also show that it can be exchanged with dense attention before or after training. Applications to pretrained language and vision models produce reported memory and speed benefits, making the approximation useful beyond models built specifically around it.

In one result, SMYRF-BERT slightly outperforms BERT on GLUE while using 50% less memory. The authors also use SMYRF to train BigGAN on Celeba-HQ with attention at resolutions of 128 by 128 and 256 by 256 on a single TPU, generating realistic faces. These examples demonstrate both adapting existing models and enabling high-resolution attention during training.
neurips-2020-smyrf-efficient-attention-u.tldr: SMYRF approximates attention through balanced asymmetric clustering, reducing complexity and memory use while supporting pretrained models without retraining.

paragraphs: Physical environments can change without announcing a new task. This paper develops an online, model-based reinforcement-learning approach for that situation, without requiring pretraining or known task boundaries. It addresses settings where assumptions about independent tasks, accessible task distributions, or clear task divisions do not hold.

The method maintains a mixture of expert models, using a Gaussian Process for each different type of dynamics. These models reuse collected data and represent uncertainty. A transition prior captures temporal dependencies in the incoming stream, while sequential variational inference updates the mixture as observations arrive. The system creates models for unfamiliar dynamics and reuses existing models when familiar dynamics return.

Experiments cover classic control with changing dynamics and decision-making across driving scenarios. The authors report better performance than alternative methods on these nonstationary tasks. The results support combining uncertainty-aware dynamics models with online model creation and reuse as a way to adapt across changing tasks without explicit signals marking their boundaries.
neurips-2020-task-agnostic-online-reinfo.tldr: An online mixture of Gaussian Process dynamics models adapts to unannounced task changes by creating new experts and reusing familiar ones.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning method may learn a task efficiently for several reasons, including better representations and model-based learning. Measuring sample efficiency on a single task blends those contributions together. This paper introduces an experimental setup designed to assess model-based behavior more directly, inspired by neuroscience studies of humans and animals.

The associated metric, Local Change Adaptation regret, measures how quickly a method adapts after a local change in the environment. The authors argue that it can identify model-based behavior even when the method has a poor representation. It also provides insight into how closely the observed behavior approaches optimal model-based behavior.

The paper applies the setup to MuZero on a variation of Mountain Car. The abstract presents this as an evaluation application without stating a particular outcome for MuZero. The broader contribution is the diagnostic question the setup makes measurable: how effectively does a method adapt to a localized environmental change, beyond what its original task-learning speed alone reveals?
neurips-2020-the-loca-regret-a-consisten.tldr: LoCA regret measures adaptation to local environmental changes to help distinguish model-based behavior from other sources of learning efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper develops Bayesian methods for learning directed acyclic graphs and their implied causal effects from complete, passively observed data. It builds on a Markov chain Monte Carlo approach that approximately samples graph structures from their posterior distribution. That approach is efficient when each node has a small set of candidate parents.

The authors reduce the method's time and memory requirements, making substantially larger candidate-parent sets feasible. They also study how to choose those candidates so that the allowed graph structures cover as much posterior probability as possible. This addresses both the cost of searching possible structures and the consequences of restricting the search.

The graph sampler is then combined with a new Bayesian method for estimating causal effects in linear Gaussian DAG models. Numerical experiments demonstrate performance in detecting ancestor-descendant relations, and the causal-effect method outperforms previous approaches in the reported evaluations. The work therefore links more scalable uncertainty over graph structure with causal-effect estimation under the specified model family.
neurips-2020-towards-scalable-bayesian-l.tldr: More efficient Bayesian graph sampling supports larger candidate-parent sets and improves reported causal-effect estimation in linear Gaussian DAG models.
